title: Noise-floor plot: is the difference bigger than noise?
summary: Before claiming that a variant is better, ask whether the difference is bigger than the run-to-run noise. The plot shows every seed of each variant, the mean, and a noise floor taken from the spread of the baseline over its seeds.

media.alt: Dot plot of a metric against four variants: baseline, variant 1, variant 2, variant 3, each with ten scattered markers and a white mean bar; a horizontal rose dashed line at 0.810 labelled noise floor with a shaded rose band below it; variants 1 and 2 sit inside the band, variant 3 clearly above.
media.caption: Reference render of class F8.6 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Is the difference bigger than noise?
read_the_figure.axes: x: four categories (baseline, variant 1, 2, 3), with markers jittered sideways. y: metric (higher is better), from 0.785 to 0.86, ten seeds per variant. A dashed line marks the noise floor and the band below it is the baseline mean plus or minus two standard deviations.
look_at: Which variants lie clearly above the noise floor, and which are inside the band?
How spread out are the seeds within one variant, compared with the gaps between variant means?
How is the floor defined (here: baseline mean plus two standard deviations over seeds)?
Are all seeds drawn, or only the means?
as_drawn: Ten seeds per variant (jittered markers) and a white bar at each mean: baseline 0.800, variant 1 about 0.804, variant 2 about 0.809, variant 3 about 0.836.
The floor is stated in the legend: baseline mean plus two standard deviations over seeds, 0.810, so the baseline standard deviation is about 0.005.

Variants 1 and 2 are inside the shaded band (0.790 to 0.810) and labelled not distinguishable from noise. Variant 3 lies above the floor with every seed at 0.829 or higher and is labelled above floor.
The band is a threshold for single runs. Means of ten seeds are about three times tighter, so the band is conservative for comparing means (see below).
read_the_figure.proves: Variant 3 beats the baseline by far more than the seed-to-seed noise, so it is a real improvement for this setup. For variants 1 and 2 the plot says only that single runs are not distinguishable; it is conservative, and a test on the means may still find a small real difference.
if_wrong: Only means plotted: the noise cannot be judged.
A floor with no stated definition: the reader cannot reproduce it.
A variant mean just inside the band declared equal to the baseline: absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
must_check: floor line: the floor is the yardstick against which a difference is judged, so it must be drawn and defined.

terms.meaning: The initial state of the random number generator; changing it changes initial weights and data order.
The variation of the metric between seeds for the same method.
A threshold, here baseline mean plus two standard deviations, below which a single run cannot be called better than the baseline.
s divided by the square root of the number of seeds.
A test for a difference of two means that does not assume equal variances.
Testing several variants against the baseline raises the chance of a false positive; the threshold must be tightened.

remember: Floor = baseline mean + 2 s over seeds (for single runs).
Means of n seeds are tighter: SE = s / sqrt(n); the SE of a difference of two means is s sqrt(2 / n).
Compare means with Welch's t, or a rank test, not with the single-run band.
Three variants against one baseline: use a corrected threshold.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position on y is the metric, one marker per seed, jittered sideways so overlapping values stay visible. The white bar is each variant's mean. The dashed line and the shaded band come from the baseline's own spread, so the yardstick is built from the same data type. Marker shape and colour separate the variants and a text label says which are above or inside the band.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: if you rerun the same method ten times you get ten slightly different scores. A new method is only better if its scores are clearly higher than that wobble. Showing all ten scores and a line at the top of the baseline's wobble puts the question on the page: is the cloud of the new variant above the line? The jitter and the bar show the spread and the centre together.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: The band applies to single runs, but conclusions usually concern means. With ten seeds the standard error of a mean difference is 0.0023 here, so variant 2, whose mean is 0.0086 above the baseline, is about 3.8 standard errors away (Welch p = 0.016) although it sits inside the band. Conversely a threshold of two baseline standard deviations is fixed by ten baseline runs, which are themselves noisy. Three variants compared with one baseline need a stricter level than 0.05.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Report the difference of means with a confidence interval for each variant and compare it with zero (F7.6 does this for ablations). Use paired seeds when the variants share initial conditions. A bootstrap interval of the difference makes no normality assumption. Increase the number of seeds when a small difference matters.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add the 95 percent interval of each mean as a thick bar, replace the single-run band by the interval of the difference from the baseline, and print the Welch p-value and the corrected threshold under each variant.

steps.title: The noise floor and its meaning
steps.note: A single run of the baseline falls below the floor about 97.5 percent of the time if the scores are roughly normal.

steps.title: Comparing means instead of single runs
steps.note: With 10 seeds: variant 1 (difference 0.004) has z of about 1.9, variant 2 (0.0086) about 3.8 and variant 3 (0.036) about 16.

steps.title: Tests with a correction for three comparisons
steps.note: Welch tests on the render's seeds (scratch script). Variant 2 passes the corrected level barely, so it is suggestive but fragile; variant 1 does not pass.

worked.title: Reading the noise-floor plot of the reference render
worked.problem: (1) What is the baseline's standard deviation implied by the floor? (2) By how many standard deviations does variant 3 exceed the floor, and how many standard errors of a difference is its gap from the baseline? (3) Variant 2 lies inside the band; can its mean still differ from the baseline?

solution.text: (1) The floor of 0.810 is the baseline mean (0.800) plus two standard deviations.
(2) Variant 3 has a mean of about 0.836.
(3) Yes: for variant 2 the difference of the means is about 0.0086.
So the single-run band says 'not distinguishable per run' but the means of ten seeds may still differ; at a corrected level of 0.0167 the result is borderline.

worked.answer: s of 0.005; variant 3 is 5 standard deviations above the floor and about 16 SE from the baseline mean; variant 2's mean difference is about 3.8 SE, borderline significant after correction.

analyze.q: Why can a variant be inside the noise band for single runs yet still be significantly better in the mean?
What would you do before declaring variant 2 an improvement?
analyze.hint: More seeds, corrected threshold, a second dataset.

analyze.q: The floor is defined from ten baseline runs. How reliable is it?
analyze.hint: Uncertainty of a standard deviation from ten values.

evaluate.q: A figure shows only variant means with a line at the baseline. What is missing?

create: Add the 95 percent interval of each variant mean and the Welch p-value beneath each label.
Rerun with 30 seeds and see which variants leave the band.

checks.hint: A threshold from the baseline's own spread.
checks.answer: The baseline mean plus two seed standard deviations: a single run of a variant below it cannot be called better than the baseline.

checks.q: s = 0.006 and n = 10 seeds per method. What is the standard error of a difference of two means?
A mean sits inside the band but the Welch p is 0.01 for three variants. What do you report?
checks.answer: Report that single runs overlap the baseline but the means differ by about 3 to 4 SE; the p of 0.01 is borderline against the corrected 0.0167 for three variants, so more seeds are needed before claiming an improvement.
